**What I learned:**

I learnt about ARCH and GARCH modelling in R and how these models describe conditional variance and its changes over time. I understood that autoregressive models can still be used to model the conditional mean, while ARCH/GARCH models describe the conditional variance of the innovations. These models are commonly used in financial applications to capture changes in volatility.

I also learnt about the stylized facts of financial returns, which are patterns commonly observed in financial data, such as volatility clustering. An ARCH model represents the conditional variance as a function of past squared innovations, whereas a GARCH model also includes lagged conditional variances. I learnt that these models describe the variance of innovations from a mean model, which we estimate using residuals. Transforming financial prices into returns is a separate data preparation step and is different from obtaining residuals. I also learnt about common pitfalls when fitting and assessing ARCH/GARCH models.

In R, I worked through the modelling process step by step, from preparing the data to fitting, checking and selecting a model. The session also emphasized that the GARCH family is large. Although we mainly covered GARCH(1,1), there are many other specifications to explore. I look forward to investigating some of these in my time series project and applying this knowledge in my future career.

**Follow-up — 18 September 2026:**

I revisited my understanding of the ARCH-LM test and realized that I had confused testing for ARCH effects with testing for normality. The ARCH-LM test checks whether past squared residuals help explain current squared residuals, rather than whether the residuals follow a normal distribution.

Before fitting a volatility model, the test can provide evidence of ARCH effects. After fitting an ARCH/GARCH model, applying it to the standardized residuals helps assess whether ARCH effects remain. A significant result suggests that the fitted model has not fully captured the conditional variance dynamics. A non-significant result means there is insufficient evidence of remaining ARCH effects, rather than proving that the model is correct.
